new.title: MAIC-2 v2.3: A Fortran program for simulating the surface temperature, atmospheric water transport and surface glaciation of the planet Mars
new.summary: The Mars Atmosphere-Ice Coupler MAIC-2 is a computationally efficient, zonally-averaged model designed to simulate Martian surface temperature, atmospheric water transport and surface glaciation over timescales of 10^5 to 10^7 years. While sophisticated General Circulation Models (GCMs) provide high-resolution simulations of the Martian atmosphere, their high computational cost makes them largely unsuitable for studies covering millions of years of orbital evolution. MAIC-2 addresses this gap by utilizing physically-based, zonally-averaged parameterizations, including a Local Insolation Temperature (LIT) scheme and a mass balance engine driven by free-convection and instantaneous mixing physics. Version 2.3 introduces a fully modularized Fortran architecture that improves maintainability and ensures that the software remains entirely self-contained, requiring no external numerical libraries or specialized data formats for execution. Demonstrated through a 20-million-year transient simulation, the model successfully reproduces the primary characteristics of the Martian polar layered deposits. MAIC-2 provides the planetary science community with a versatile, open-source tool for investigating the long-term climatic impacts of orbital variations on the Martian surface.

figures.caption: Modular structure of MAIC-2 v2.3. All initializations are done in the main program maic2 . This includes reading the physical parameters and the set-up from the run-specs header file maic2_specs_<run_name>.h , where <run_name> is a placeholder for the name of the simulation to be carried out. In the main loop (numerical forward-in-time integration), maic2 carries out three steps: (1) Use the module boundary_maic2_m to update the orbital parameters, compute the surface temperature (LIT scheme, module instemp_m ) and the surface mass balance for H 2 O ice (evaporation, atmospheric water transport and condensation, module evap_cond_m ); (2) use the module calc_top_maic2_m to update the topography (thickness) of the H 2 O ice deposits; (3) use the module output_m for data output in ASCII format. Auxiliary modules are maic2_types_m for declarations of kind types, maic2_variables_m for declarations of global variables, and maic2_maths_m for required mathematical tools.

new.title: NEXONN: Advancing the NEXOTRANS Exoplanet Atmospheric Retrieval Framework with Transformer-Based Neural Posterior Estimation for JWST Transmission Spectroscopy of WASP-39b
new.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope is delivering unprecedented constraints on exoplanet atmospheres, but computationally intensive Bayesian retrievals challenge the transition from individual planets to population-level studies of planetary formation and evolution. We introduce NEXONN, a transformer-conditioned normalizing-flow framework within NEXOTRANS that enables rapid atmospheric posterior estimation with uncertainty quantification. Incorporating PandExo-based JWST noise, we benchmark NEXONN against PyMultiNest using simulated spectra and JWST observations of WASP-39 b (0.6-12 microns). For simulated MIRI/LRS data, eight posteriors achieve a mean overlap of 80.32%. Retrievals of combined NIRISS, NIRSpec, and MIRI observations yield consistent atmospheric properties. For the full dataset, NEXONN infers C/O = 0.82 (+0.01/-0.02) and [M/H] = 1.13 (+0.04/-0.04), compared with PyMultiNest values of 0.80 (+0.03/-0.01) and 1.19 (+0.05/-0.03). Divergence metrics, Wasserstein distances, posterior overlaps, and coverage tests assess posterior fidelity and uncertainty calibration, revealing parameter-dependent differences. Once trained, NEXONN performs posterior inference within seconds, enabling scalable population studies of exoplanet atmospheric composition, formation, and evolution.

figures.caption: Overview of the NEXOTRANS framework [ 12 ] , showing the forward-modeling component (green box), existing retrieval methods (purple box), and the NEXONN framework introduced in this work (gray box). The forward model generates transmission spectra by solving the radiative-transfer equation for specified atmospheric properties, including chemical composition, pressure–temperature structure, and cloud prescriptions. The existing retrieval module includes Bayesian sampling methods such as PyMultiNest and UltraNest , together with the machine-learning-based Stacking Regressor, which combines Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and K-Nearest Neighbors. NEXONN extends this framework using TcNF to perform probabilistic posterior estimation of atmospheric parameters.

new.title: Asgard/NOTT: L-band nulling interferometry at the VLTI IV. Prospects for characterising hot exozodiacal dust
new.summary: Near-infrared interferometric surveys have revealed extended emission around the photosphere of $\approx 40$ main-sequence stars, attributed to the presence of hot exozodiacal dust (HEZD). A promising technique for investigating this phenomenon is nulling interferometry. The Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) nulling interferometer NOTT (Nulling Observations of exoplaneTs and dusT) is designed to characterise exoplanets and HEZD in the $L'$ band ($3.5-4.0\,\mu$m). We aim to assess NOTT's potential for the detection and characterisation of HEZD with various instrumental and model parameter configurations. We model the HEZD as an optically thin dust ring, using the nearby Sun-like star $\tau$ Ceti with HEZD as a reference model. Applying the end-to-end nulling tool SCIFYsim to model the instrumental response of NOTT to simulated HEZD brightness distributions, we evaluate how variations in HEZD and instrumental parameters affect NOTT's key observables: the photon flux rate and the null depth. We demonstrate that NOTT is capable of disentangling stellar and dust contributions to the signal and detecting HEZD. The null depth and photon flux rate are sensitive to the HEZD geometry, with inclination, position angle, and ring location having the strongest impact on the signal. Although the detailed temporal signatures are target-specific, the results can be generalised to other systems. NOTT has the potential to deliver unprecedented sensitivity for HEZD observations, granting access to detailed information through spectral dispersion, beam-combination schemes, and exploitation of sky rotation. This enables more sensitive HEZD detections than is possible with current instruments, and improved spatial constraints on the dust, as well as variability studies.

new.title: Analytical formulae for planet-planet or moon-moon tides
new.summary: Almost negligible among the solar system planets, mutual tides raised by a secondary on another secondary orbiting the same primary may gain increased importance in tightly packed systems, e.g., between the components of close-in exoplanetary systems or between the moons of gas giants. In this work, we derive an analytical formula for the planet-planet tidal potential and for the effect of mutual tides on the rotational and orbital evolution of moons or planets in a coplanar configuration. The procedure follows closely the steps of W. M. Kaula (1961), and the resulting potential and derived quantities are presented in the form of an expansion into modes of different frequencies (in the temporal domain) and spherical harmonic components (in the spatial domain). The analytical formulae are implemented into a code and compared with an independent numerical solution.

new.title: Thermodynamics of gas giants accreting via shocks: the role of molecular hydrogen dissociation
new.summary: Within the core-accretion framework, gas giants acquire most of their mass through accretion shocks during runaway gas accretion. The shock thermodynamics---governed by radiative cooling, accretion history, and equation of state (EoS)---sets the post-shock gas entropy and initial thermal state, strongly influencing both observables and subsequent evolution. We aim to build a coupled evolutionary model predicting the initial thermodynamic conditions, intrinsic luminosities, and upper limits on magnetic field strengths of gas giants across diverse accretion histories. We couple radiation hydrodynamics and $\mathrm{H_2}$ dissociation to long-term planetary interior evolution by training a physics-informed neural network (PINN) predictor on 1000 first-principles simulations resolving the shock physics. This PINN provides post-shock outer boundary conditions for MESA to evolve the planetary envelope beyond runaway accretion. The PINN predicts higher post-shock temperatures than the canonical cold-start model, with the discrepancy widening with planetary mass, while post-shock entropy jumps sharply when $\mathrm{H_2}$ dissociates at $\sim 2000$ K. Gas giants evolved with PINN-derived boundary conditions achieve intrinsic luminosities 4--10 times higher than cold-start models. Under optimistic assumptions, the maximum magnetic field strength at $2 R_{\mathrm{J}}$ reaches a few gauss for a $0.3 M_{\mathrm{J}}$ planet, $\sim 100$ G for $1 M_{\mathrm{J}}$, and $\sim 500$ G for $3 M_{\mathrm{J}}$. Incorporating detailed radiation hydrodynamics and realistic thermodynamics into accretion shock models yields higher initial entropies, brighter intrinsic luminosities, and stronger magnetic fields, providing improved constraints on the masses and accretion rates of directly imaged exoplanets.

new.title: Potential spectral markers of intrinsic magnetic fields of hot exoplanets in the UV range
new.summary: A method for detecting the intrinsic magnetic fields of exoplanets, based on the effect of atomic alignment (the redistribution of populations among magnetic sublevels under the action of anisotropic radiation from the host star), has been adapted for observations with the Spektr-UV space telescope. A procedure for selecting sensitive transitions is proposed, and triplet absorption lines in the UV range that are sensitive to alignment are identified. On the basis of three-dimensional aeronomic models of the hot Jupiters KELT-20 b and HAT-P-32 b, absorption spectra in these lines are calculated for cases with and without intrinsic magnetic fields of the exoplanets. Using the Spektr-UV exposure-time calculator, the observability of the effect is assessed, and an observing program is proposed, specifying the optimal duration of individual exposures and the number of transits required to detect the signal.

new.title: A Homogeneous Benchmark of Exoplanet Mass-Radius Relations
new.summary: The mass-radius ($M$-$R$) relation is fundamental to inferring the bulk composition and internal structure of exoplanets. However, published relations remain difficult to compare directly because studies adopt different planetary samples, fitting procedures, and evaluation metrics. We construct a homogeneous, quality-controlled benchmark of 963 exoplanets with dynamically measured masses and transit radii from the NASA Exoplanet Archive. We compare empirical power laws, probabilistic models, and machine-learning (ML) regressors using point accuracy, interval coverage, and probabilistic calibration. On the full test set, a multi-feature random forest has the lowest root-mean-square error, 0.329~dex in $\log_{10} M$ versus 0.368~dex for a fitted two-parameter power law ($p = 0.007$ unadjusted; $p = 0.059$ after Holm correction across 13 comparisons). Radius-only ML models perform comparably to the single power law. In three ranges of the measured radius, several methods improve on the power law below 1.6 $R_\oplus$, but none does between 1.6 and 4 $R_\oplus$. Including stellar and orbital covariates significantly improves predictions only for low-mass planets ($M < 4.4\,M_\oplus$), although this result is sensitive to missing covariate data and weakens when the training and test sets are separated by host star. Within their calibrated radius domains, the published empirical and probabilistic relations remain highly competitive. Finally, a first-order variance decomposition shows that formal measurement uncertainties account for only $\sim$3\% of the residual variance (0.067 of 0.401~dex), and the remaining $\sim$0.396~dex arises from compositional diversity, selection effects, and model approximation error.

new.title: Discovery of a Massive Outer Companion to the TOI-178 Resonant Chain
new.summary: We report the discovery of a massive outer companion around TOI-178, a known planetary system with six inner small planets within 0.15 AU, five of which are in a 2:4:6:9:12 resonant chain. We analyse the astrometric anomalies in the combined Gaia DR2/DR3 - Hipparcos catalogue (G23H) and literature radial velocities, revealing strong evidence for a massive outer companion at several AU. We combine the resulting orbital fit posterior with archival high-contrast imaging to constrain the properties of the corresponding massive outer companion, TOI-178 h. We also study the dynamical stability of the inner resonant chain in the presence of this previously unknown outer companion via both heuristic and N-body simulations. We find that the inner system appears to be robust to the perturbing influence of TOI-178\,h, in line with the systems several Gyr age. Our analysis results in a final posterior solution for TOI-178\,h with a semi-major axis of $6.9^{+12.3}_{-3.3}$ AU, a mass of $21^{+47}_{-11} M_J$, and eccentricity of $0.76^{+0.18}_{-0.35}$, likely corresponding to an eccentric brown dwarf. TOI-178 is currently the only known system that has maintained a high-multiplicity resonant chain whilst in the dynamical presence of a massive outer companion, showcasing a unique outcome of planet formation.

cross.title: Lunar laser ranging analyses of NGLR-1 data with PEP and prospects for MPAc: towards one millimeter range precision
cross.summary: Since 1969, Lunar Laser Ranging (LLR) has provided critical data for investigating Earth-Moon dynamics, lunar internal structure, and tests of General Relativity (GR). However, the measurement precision of historical arrays (such as those from Apollo and Lunokhod missions) is inherently limited by laser pulse broadening induced by lunar librations. To overcome this limit, next-generation single Cube Corner Retroreflectors (CCRs) of large optical diameter have been developed to eliminate pulse dispersion, enabling LLR measurements to advance from centimeter-level precision down to the millimeter scale. In this work, we present a detailed analysis of LLR observations from NGLR-1 (Next Generation Lunar Retroreflector-1), the first single 10cm-diameter CCR deployed on the lunar surface. Carried out using the Planetary Ephemeris Program (PEP), this study investigates individual range measurements, normal points (NPs), residuals, and observational dispersion collected by the ground stations at Apache Point Observatory Lunar laser ranging station (APOL), Wettzell, and Grasse. The results: demonstrate the success of NGLR-1 in significantly enhancing time of flight measurement precision compared to legacy Apollo and Lunokhod retroreflector arrays; indicate similar good prospects also for ESA's MPAc laser retroreflector (MoonLIGHT with Pointing Actuators) to be launched in early 2027; pave the way for a new era of LLR observations and enhanced tests of GR, alternative gravity theories in general and improved lunar geophysics and geodesy.

cross.title: Enabling joint chemical and meteorological data assimilation with an atmospheric foundation model
cross.summary: The hydroxyl radical (OH) is the main oxidant in the troposphere and accounts for 88% of the methane sink, yet its abundance and trends remain poorly constrained. Satellites observe many of the chemical and meteorological drivers of OH, but assimilating both requires a model that represents chemistry and meteorology together. Existing chemistry-climate models are too expensive for joint data assimilation. Here, we present AuroraChem, a fine-tuned version of the Aurora atmospheric foundation model that jointly simulates meteorology and the GEOS-Chem chemical fields needed to constrain OH. A one-year AuroraChem rollout takes 12 minutes on one GPU. Free rollouts remain stable for one year but do not fully capture seasonal cycles. Using idealized data assimilation, we find that chemical observations can constrain the meteorological state and meteorological observations can constrain the chemical state. Inserting only the chemical fields raises the annual mean spatial correlation of 500 hPa temperature from 0.89 to 0.92 and recovers the moisture and circulation pattern of the Indian summer monsoon. Inserting only the meteorological fields raises the 500 hPa OH correlation from 0.89 to 0.93, close to the 0.94 from inserting the chemical fields themselves, and recovers the OH seasonal cycle. Inserting only NO2 columns sampled at TROPOMI pixels gives an OH correlation of 0.93. These relationships likely reflect learned covariances rather than physical coupling, and covariances are what data assimilation uses to let an observation of one variable update the others. AuroraChem therefore provides a new pathway to joint chemical and meteorological data assimilation.

repl.title: An Outer Giant Excites and Constrains the Orbit of $π$ Mensae d
repl.summary: The nearby $\pi$ Mensae system contains the eccentric giant planet b on a 5.7 yr orbit, the 6.27 day transiting sub-Neptune c, and a candidate planet d on a 123 day orbit between them. Published estimates place the eccentricity of d between approximately 0.2 and 0.4. We reanalyze 772 published velocities with three-Keplerian fits and explore three-dimensional b-d dynamics with $N$-body integrations. The high-eccentricity solution persists when the phase or apsidal prior is widened; exact importance reweighting to a population-informed Beta eccentricity prior gives $e_d=0.378^{+0.050}_{-0.049}$. In 20 kyr integrations, 84.5% of configurations near the prograde and retrograde coplanar endpoints survive, compared with 21.3% across $60^\circ\leq I_{bd}<120^\circ$; stellar collisions dominate the failures. Secular forcing by b moves 53 of 62 one-Myr survivors initialized with $e_d\leq0.1$ into $0.3\leq e_d\leq0.5$. Representative b+d configurations remain viable for 100 Myr, whereas controls with c and general relativity retain fewer systems. The outer giant can therefore excite the observed eccentricity of d while constraining its viable orbit toward prograde or retrograde near-coplanar configurations.

repl.title: Detailed study of HD 219134: A benchmark K dwarf with a compact planetary system
repl.summary: Space missions such as CoRoT, Kepler, and TESS have transformed asteroseismology and its synergies with exoplanet science. We revisit the nearby K-dwarf HD 219134 to investigate the tension between asteroseismic and interferometric radii, update its fundamental parameters, and reconstruct the rotational, magnetic, and atmospheric evolution of the system. We combine forward asteroseismic modeling with seismic inversions to assess systematics from non-seismic constraints, radius measurements, and surface modeling. The revised stellar properties are then used for rotational evolution, stellar-wind, and high-energy irradiation calculations. Seismic inversions rule out the most recent interferometric radius, while the asteroseismic and spectroscopic results are compatible with the 2019 interferometric measurement. We obtain $M=0.779\pm0.015_\mathrm{(stat)}\pm0.006_\mathrm{(sys)}\ M_\odot$, $R=0.753\pm0.005_\mathrm{(stat)}\pm0.002_\mathrm{(sys)}\ R_\odot$, and an age of $8.92\pm0.89_\mathrm{(stat)}\pm0.19_\mathrm{(sys)}$ Gyr. These systematics include only non-seismic constraints; literature combined uncertainties from physical inputs and surface effects are $0.007M_\odot$, $0.002R_\odot$, and $0.81$ Gyr. Rotational and wind modelling shows that standard magnetic braking is broadly compatible with the present-day rotation and angular-momentum loss. Weakened braking gives a closer match but challenges standard wind-loss scalings. The inferred X-ray history suggests early stripping of the innermost planets, while the outer planets likely retained part of their primordial envelopes; HD 219134d experienced only moderate erosion. The apparent radius discrepancy likely reflects underestimated uncertainties in previous interferometric analyses rather than an astrophysical inconsistency. We advocate adopting the asteroseismic radius, which is robust to modeling assumptions and optimisation strategies.

repl.title: Thermodynamically consistent equation of state tables for use in giant planet and brown dwarf interior modeling
repl.summary: Equation of state (EOS) tables used in giant planet modeling exhibit regions of strong thermodynamic inconsistency, or disobedience to the first law of thermodynamics. These generally result from smooth interpolation over physical discontinuities or between thermodynamic sub-domains governed by different physical models. The effect of thermodynamic inconsistency on structure models of planets evolved with these EOS has never been studied in detail, although it is understood to introduce spurious sources or sinks of energy or entropy in the models, leading to inaccuracies. Here, we present a method for improving the thermodynamic consistency of an existing EOS table, based on constructing a Helmholtz free energy $F(\rho,T)$ covering the EOS domain and deriving all the other necessary EOS quantities from it. This method produces EOS tables with roughly thousandfold better thermodynamic consistency across the EOS domain of interest, as quantified by three thermodynamic consistency metrics derived from the first law. We also present a controlled experiment comparing giant planet models evolved with MESA using the original EOS and the $F$-derived, thermodynamically consistent versions, and find that the models can differ by up to $5\%$ in radius at an age of 5 Gyr, and by up to $25\%$ in luminosity at earlier stages of evolution; thermodynamic consistency is thus an especially important consideration for characterising young directly imaged planets. We present the $F$-derived, thermodynamically consistent versions of the tables for download at \href{ this https URL }{ this https URL }, along with example MESA inlists to reproduce our evolution models.

repl.title: The GAPS Programme at TNG LXXXI. The puzzle of the HeI absorption signal in the atmosphere of V1298 Tau b with GIARPS@TNG
repl.summary: Atmospheric escape shapes close-in planets mostly in their first tens of Myr. The young V1298Tau system (10-30Myr) is a benchmark for investigating photoevaporation and planetary evolution at early stages. The metastable HeI near-infrared triplet is a key proxy for atmospheric escape. We aim to detect and characterise HeI in the extended atmosphere of V1298Taub. We analysed four transits over a 4-year baseline using GIARPS (GIANO-B + HARPS-N) at the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo. We re-derived the projected spin-orbit angle by modelling the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect. Using simultaneous optical and near-infrared high-resolution transmission spectroscopy of V1298Taub, we monitored the HeI triplet alongside key chromospheric indicators ($\log R'_{HK}$, H$\alpha$, and NaI) to disentangle stellar activity from planetary evaporation. While the stellar spectra show significant night-to-night variability, transmission spectroscopy reveals persistent HeI absorption across all four epochs. This contrasts with H$\alpha$ and NaI, observed over two nights with simultaneous HARPS-N monitoring, which fluctuate between emission and absorption due to stellar activity. The consistent presence of HeI over 4 years may suggest a planetary origin, despite stellar-driven depth modulation. ATES hydrodynamic simulations show that stellar XUV flux variations modulate the HeI absorption depth and equivalent width. Furthermore, stellar wind fluctuations likely drive the observed night-to-night variability of the exospheric structure. The detection of HeI across all epochs may support planetary evaporation, despite modulation by stellar activity. Our results underscore that disentangling a planetary signal from stellar contamination remains challenging for highly active hosts; securing the planetary nature of the HeI signature requires activity monitoring and full transit coverage to establish a robust baseline.

repl.title: On the Detectability of Compact Multi-Planet Systems via Gravitational Microlensing
repl.summary: Compact multi-planet systems orbiting ultracool dwarfs, such as TRAPPIST-1, may be a major population of terrestrial worlds with poorly constrained demographics. Individual close-in planets are expected to escape microlensing detection, but whether a compact system can produce a detectable collective signal remains to be quantified. We calculate the microlensing signal from each TRAPPIST-1 planet, and of all seven combined, if the system were a lens toward the bulge. For a 0.09 $M_\odot$ lens at 4 kpc, $R_E \approx 1.21$ AU, placing the planets at $s = 0.010$--$0.051~\theta_E$, 12--63 times interior to the lensing zone. We measure each signal as the residual after fitting a single-lens model, which accounts for the barycentric dipole. Because the quadrupole term cancels between the two images to first order, the residual scales as the octupole ($q s^3$), reaching $|\delta A / A| \sim 10^{-6}$. The seven planets combined yield $\Delta\chi^2 \sim 10^{-3}$ even at 1~mmag precision, five orders of magnitude below the standard detection threshold. Detection requires increasing all planet masses by a factor of $\sim$300, whereas the resonant chain loses its guarantee of Hill stability at a factor of $\sim$7. Only a lens within $\sim$15 pc of the source or the Sun places the outer planets in the lensing zone. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is therefore not expected to detect a TRAPPIST-1-like system through microlensing, whereas its transit channel in the same fields can detect such planets in large numbers, marking a sharp boundary in the Galactic census between microlensing and transit sensitivity.

repl.title: Constraining Ganymede's Interior Structure and Bulk Composition from Its Present-Day Magnetic Field Strength
repl.summary: Ganymede is the only Solar System satellite with a global magnetic field driven by a core dynamo. Although its small moment-of-inertia (MoI) factor indicates a differentiated structure of a metallic core, rocky mantle, and outer hydrosphere, its exact bulk composition and layer thicknesses remain highly uncertain. We developed a comprehensive, long-term thermochemical evolution model that couples thermal history with magnetic field generation. Building upon previous theoretical frameworks, this study systematically evaluates how diverse chondritic precursor compositions constrain Ganymede's internal thermochemical evolution and core solidification processes. Based on interior structures initially permitted by a wide range of chondritic compositions and geodetic constraints, we applied the observed equatorial surface magnetic field strength ($\sim$719 nT) as a dynamic filter. Our evolutionary simulations demonstrate that while magnetic dynamos can operate under entire melting, Fe-snow, and FeS-layer regimes, the requirement to sustain the observed field strength strongly restricts the viable interior models. Satisfying this constraint preferentially requires a relatively large core radius and a specific, non-eutectic bulk core sulfur concentration. Consequently, this coupled thermochemical approach highlights the main novelty of this study: characterizing the hydrosphere's density serves as an independent constraint to break the structural degeneracy of Ganymede's bulk composition. Our model indicates that L and CI chondrites yield parameter spaces capable of sustaining comparable field strengths under a low-density hydrosphere scenario (1,200 kg m-3), whereas the H chondrite composition can satisfy this criterion under a high-density scenario (1,300 kg m-3). These predictions provide a critical framework to be tested by the JUICE mission arriving in 2031.

repl.title: On the synergetic use of Ariel and JWST for exoplanet atmospheric science
repl.summary: This paper explores the potential for strategic synergies between the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Ariel Space Telescope, two flagship observatories poised to revolutionise the study of exoplanet atmospheres. Both telescopes have the potential to address common fundamental questions about exoplanets---especially concerning their nature and origins---and serve a growing scientific community. With their operations now anticipated to overlap from 2031, there is a unique opportunity to enhance the scientific outputs of both observatories through coordinated efforts. In this report, authored by the Ariel-JWST Synergy Working Group, part of the Ariel Consortium Science Team, we summarise the capabilities of both telescopes; we highlight their key differences, similarities, synergies, and distinctive strengths. Ariel is designed to conduct a broad survey of exoplanet atmospheres but remains highly flexible, allowing the mission to integrate insights from JWST's discoveries. Findings from JWST, including data from initiatives shaped by NASA's decadal survey priorities and community-driven research themes, will inform the development of Ariel's survey strategy. Conversely, Ariel's broad-wavelength coverage for bright targets provides complementary avenues for exoplanet researchers, particularly those interested in time-domain observations and large-scale atmospheric studies. We identify key pathways for fostering JWST-Ariel synergies, many of which can be initiated even before Ariel's launch. Leveraging their complementary designs and scopes, JWST and Ariel can jointly address fundamental questions about the nature, formation, and evolution of exoplanets. Such collaboration has the potential to maximise the scientific returns of both observatories and lay the foundation for future facilities in the roadmap to exoplanet exploration.

repl.title: Assessing the enrichment of heat-producing elements in deep-mantle structures using a directional geoneutrino detector
repl.summary: Determining the spatial distribution of heat-producing elements (HPEs) within the Earth is critical for understanding the planet's thermal and chemical evolution. A central debate is whether domains in the deep mantle, particularly the Large Low-Velocity Provinces (LLVP), represent anomalous, radiogenically enriched reservoirs. Variation in the surface flux of geoneutrinos provide a direct probe of Earth's internal radioactivity. However, current continental located detectors measure only the angle-integrated flux, leading to strong spatial trade-offs that substantially limit the ability of practical networks to uniquely resolve mantle compositional heterogeneity. In this study, we quantify the potential of directional geoneutrino detection to overcome this limitation. By evaluating realistic LLVP geometries in the context of the proposed Ocean Bottom Detector (OBD), we demonstrate that resolving the incoming direction of geoneutrinos can substantially improve the precision with which HPE enrichment in LLVPs can be constrained relative to the surrounding mantle, for a range of target angular resolutions envisioned for a future directional geoneutrino detector. These results indicate that future directional geoneutrino measurements could help determine whether LLVP host enhanced HPE abundances and assess their contribution to Earth's radiogenic heat budget. Such measurements would provide a new observational constraint on the chemical heterogeneity of the deep mantle and its role in Earth's long-term thermal evolution.
